item.text:
Below are drafting issues in the supplied text, including substantive loopholes and enforcement gaps. Potential legal challenges are identified as risks, not conclusions that the bill would be invalid.

### Section 2 — Definitions

1. **§§ 2(1)(B), 6 — “Secretary” is undefined.** Section 2 assigns designation authority to “the Secretary,” while section 6 expressly names the Secretary of State. Specify the Secretary of Commerce for domestic implementation and identify any delegable responsibilities.

2. **§ 2(1)(A) — “Single training run” invites fragmentation.** Companies could divide development into multiple subthreshold runs, checkpoints, or sequential training stages. The bill provides no aggregation rule for related development activities.

3. **§ 2(1)(A) — Distributed training is not expressly aggregated.** A developer could argue that work divided among facilities, providers, affiliates, or countries constitutes separate runs. Define a run by the coordinated training undertaking, rather than infrastructure or corporate boundaries.

4. **§ 2(1)(A) — Combining separately trained models may evade the compute trigger.** Ensembles, model merging, and systems coordinating multiple models could exceed the intended capability limit without any constituent model crossing the threshold. Such systems would depend on a separate capability designation under paragraph (B).

5. **§ 2(1)(A) — Treatment of post-training work is unclear.** The text does not specify whether fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, continual learning, distillation, or related stages count toward training compute. Developers could characterize substantial capability development as a separate or nontraining activity.

6. **§ 2(1)(A) — Inference-time capability gains are outside the compute trigger.** Large inference budgets, agent scaffolding, tools, and external memory can improve system capabilities without increasing the model’s training compute. Paragraph (B) supplies a potential backstop, but only through a Secretary’s determination.

7. **§ 2(1)(A) — Compute accounting lacks a standard.** “Quantity of computing power” ordinarily describes a rate, but the threshold measures total operations; the text also leaves operation counting, numerical precision, sparse computation, and specialized hardware unresolved. These uncertainties could produce inconsistent compliance calculations and evidentiary disputes.

8. **§ 2(1)(A) — The threshold is strict and static.** Exactly \(10^{26}\) operations is outside “greater than,” and improving algorithmic efficiency could allow increasingly capable systems below the threshold. There is no authority to adjust the threshold or adopt equivalent measures.

9. **§ 2(1) — Core technical terms and system boundaries are undefined.** “Artificial intelligence,” “model,” and “system” have no statutory definitions. Whether a product, collection of components, checkpoint, or modified version is the relevant regulated object could determine coverage.

10. **§ 2(1)(B) — Capability coverage requires an affirmative determination.** Unlike paragraph (A), paragraph (B) does not automatically cover systems meeting an objective condition. A capable subthreshold system could remain outside coverage while the Secretary lacks evidence or has not acted.

11. **§ 2(1)(B) — The capability standard is insufficiently specified.** “Substantially exceeding,” “human performance,” and “most cognitive tasks” leave the comparator, task universe, scoring, and required margin undefined. A highly dangerous system with exceptional abilities in only some domains might also fall outside the definition.

12. **§ 2(1)(B) — Evaluation conditions are unspecified.** The bill does not say whether capability is assessed with tools, scaffolding, additional compute, removed safeguards, or reasonable elicitation efforts. Results could depend on testing choices or deliberate underperformance.

13. **§ 2(1)(B) — Designation procedures and notice are missing.** There is no specified process for testing, provisional designation, notice, reconsideration, or review, nor any clear rule for when a designation becomes legally operative. Given the criminal consequences, unclear standards and notice create fair-notice and arbitrary-enforcement risks.

14. **§ 2(1) — Coverage of derivatives and transferred systems is uncertain.** The bill does not establish when a designation or training history follows a model through copying, modification, distillation, or incorporation into another system. Developers could dispute whether the resulting system remains the covered one.

15. **§ 2(2) — The extraterritorial definition omits important individuals.** “U.S. person” excludes lawful permanent residents and noncitizen U.S. nationals who are not citizens. Those individuals would not be covered by section 3 merely because of their U.S. status when acting abroad.

16. **§ 2(2) — The extraterritorial definition omits important entities.** LLCs, partnerships, trusts, and other noncorporate entities are not included, and corporations organized under federal, District of Columbia, or territorial law are not expressly included. Those omissions matter for conduct outside the United States, even where domestic conduct remains prohibited.

17. **§§ 2(2), 3(a) — Foreign affiliates and outsourcing are not expressly addressed.** Foreign subsidiaries are not U.S. persons under the definition, and the bill does not expressly prohibit directing, procuring, or financing prohibited development abroad. Existing theories of participation may reach some arrangements, but do not clearly close the gap.

18. **§ 2(3) — “Advanced AI chips” is undefined.** There are no performance, interconnect, or other criteria for determining which devices count. Enforcement would turn on an undefined hardware category that manufacturers could contest.

19. **§ 2(3) — Facility coverage can be avoided through size and distribution.** Exactly 50,000 qualifying chips is outside the definition, and large workloads can be distributed among smaller facilities. No aggregation rule covers coordinated campuses, operators, or clusters.

20. **§ 2(3) — Chip counts are an unstable proxy for computing capacity.** More capable chips, alternative accelerators, or large quantities of chips deemed not “advanced” could support covered training without triggering registration. The bill provides no capacity-based alternative or updating mechanism.

21. **§ 2(3) — Facility boundaries and location are unclear.** “Data center” is undefined, leaving room to divide a campus into nominal facilities or dispute coverage of unconventional installations. The definition also does not specify the territorial reach of the registry.

### Section 3 — Prohibition and exceptions

22. **§§ 2(1)(A), 3(a) — The compute prohibition may attach too late.** A model arguably does not become “covered” until its training has already exceeded the threshold. The text should expressly address commencing or conducting a training undertaking expected to exceed the limit, rather than relying on coverage arising during or after the prohibited act.

23. **§ 3(a) — The prohibited activities are undefined.** “Train,” “develop,” and “deploy” do not clearly distinguish research, testing, release, hosting, inference, and operation. This creates both avoidance opportunities and uncertainty for lawful activity.

24. **§ 3(a) — Continued operation is not expressly prohibited.** An operator could argue that “deploy” describes the initial placement into service, not ongoing use of an already deployed system. Express coverage of operating, maintaining in service, and making available would avoid that dispute.

25. **§ 3(a) — Transfers and enabling transactions are not expressly covered.** The bill does not separately prohibit selling or transferring model weights, licensing access, importing covered systems, or knowingly supplying essential services for prohibited activity. Some conduct may qualify as development or deployment, but the boundary is uncertain.

26. **§ 3(a) — Responsibility across the supply chain is unclear.** The text does not allocate duties among developers, cloud providers, hosts, customers, and operators of autonomous systems. Ordinary aiding-and-abetting or conspiracy law may cover some criminal participation, but does not establish a complete civil compliance framework.

27. **§ 3(a) — Cross-border deployment is ambiguous.** It is unclear when a foreign operator serving U.S. users remotely is acting “in the United States.” Conversely, the bill does not expressly address domestic access to a foreign-hosted covered system.

28. **§ 3(b) — Grandfathering exempts systems indefinitely, not merely completed work.** If any training began before enactment, the exception removes the system from all of subsection (a), including future development and deployment. A developer could initiate many projects before enactment and claim a permanent exemption for each.

29. **§ 3(b) — “Training began” has no minimum or evidentiary requirement.** A token preliminary run could support an exemption claim, and no contemporaneous registration or documentation is required. This invites disputes over backdated claims, preparatory work, and what constitutes actual commencement.

30. **§ 3(b) — Grandfathered system identity is undefined.** The bill does not say when retraining, expansion, architecture changes, new checkpoints, or descendants become a new system. A company could characterize extensive future development as continuation of an exempt project.

31. **§ 3(b) — Grandfathering lacks safety conditions or revocation.** Exempt systems need not stop scaling, undergo evaluation, restrict access, or meet security requirements. The Secretary has no express power to withdraw the exemption upon evidence of dangerous capability.

32. **§ 3(c) — The safety exception is unlimited and self-asserted.** Any actor could characterize training, development, or deployment as being “for the purpose of safety evaluation,” without prior approval or independent supervision. The exception contains no limits on scale, duration, capability, or access.

33. **§ 3(c) — Mixed-purpose and commercial activity are not addressed.** The text does not require safety evaluation to be the sole or primary purpose, or the activity to be necessary for that purpose. A commercial development program could add an evaluation component and claim exemption.

34. **§ 3(c) — No containment or release restrictions accompany the exception.** Exempt evaluations need not use secure environments, restrict replication, prevent public deployment, or control model-weight disclosure. The exception could therefore permit the very exposure the prohibition is intended to prevent.

35. **§§ 3(b)–(c), 5 — Exception administration and proof are unspecified.** No application, recordkeeping, audit, or express allocation of the burden of establishing an exception is provided. Enforcement could depend on disproving an operator’s undocumented account of its purpose or training history.

36. **§ 3(a) — Breadth creates avoidable constitutional litigation risk.** Undefined “development” could be read to encompass publication of research or code, while capability-based coverage carries severe criminal consequences. More precise conduct definitions would reduce First Amendment and vagueness challenges without necessarily exempting operational training or deployment.

### Section 4 — Registry and monitoring

37. **§ 4(a) — Registration has no deadline.** Operators are required to register, but not before operation, before crossing the facility threshold, or within a specified period. That makes delay difficult to distinguish from noncompliance.

38. **§ 4(a) — “Operator” is undefined.** Owners, lessees, cloud providers, colocation firms, and cluster managers may each argue another entity bears the duty. Shared facilities need clear responsibility rules.

39. **§ 4(b) — Reporting attaches only to registered operators.** An operator that fails to register could argue that the quarterly reporting obligation never attached. Reporting should depend on being required to register, not on having complied.

40. **§ 4(b) — Reporting timing and content are too vague.** “Quarterly” supplies no filing deadline, and “describing the computing workloads” does not require customer identities, actual compute, related runs, model identifiers, or claimed exemptions. Generic descriptions could satisfy the text while concealing violations.

41. **§ 4(b) — Quarterly reporting may arrive after prohibited work is complete.** A covered training run could begin and finish between reports. There is no advance notification, real-time threshold alert, or prompt reporting of suspected violations.

42. **§ 4 — No verification or records-access framework is provided.** Self-certification is not accompanied by required logs, retention periods, independent audits, inspections, or compulsory production authority. Commerce may be unable to establish what actually ran or substantiate an exemption claim.

43. **§§ 4–5 — Registry violations lack express penalties.** Section 5 penalizes violations of section 3, not failure to register, late reporting, or inadequate reports under section 4. General false-statement law may reach some knowingly false submissions, but does not supply a complete registry enforcement regime.

44. **§ 4 — The registry does not directly track developers or covered systems.** Prohibited activity at smaller facilities, distributed infrastructure, or exempt projects may never appear in the registry. There is no developer-level obligation to disclose aggregate compute or identify covered systems.

45. **§ 4 — Confidentiality and lawful information sharing are not specified.** Reports may contain proprietary or security-sensitive information, but the bill adds no tailored handling rules or interagency sharing framework. Existing law supplies some protections, but uncertainty could obstruct both compliance and investigation.

### Section 5 — Enforcement and penalties

46. **§§ 3–5 — No complete enforcement architecture is established.** The bill does not expressly designate a civil enforcement authority, authorize penalty assessment procedures, or specify administrative versus judicial enforcement. It also lacks general implementing-rule authority and dedicated investigative powers.

47. **§ 5 — Express preventive and emergency remedies are absent.** Monetary penalties and imprisonment do not themselves stop an ongoing run or deployment. The bill should expressly address injunctions, emergency cessation orders, and appropriately supervised measures to disable prohibited operations.

48. **§ 5(a) — The unit of violation is unclear.** “For each day on which the violation occurs” does not say whether separate systems, runs, deployments, or customers create separate violations. A company could argue for a single daily cap across extensive prohibited activity.

49. **§ 5(a) — The civil ceiling may not remove the economic incentive to violate.** The penalty is not tied to revenue, compute expenditure, or gains, and the bill expressly provides neither disgorgement nor a minimum penalty. A short violation could yield benefits far exceeding the maximum civil assessment.

50. **§ 5(a) — Civil culpability and assessment standards are unspecified.** The text does not state a knowledge standard or factors for setting penalties, such as seriousness, reasonable diligence, or repeated misconduct. Combined with uncertain coverage, this invites disputes about strict liability and inconsistent assessments.

51. **§ 5(b) — “Willfully” is not clarified.** Courts may differ over the required knowledge of unlawfulness in this regulatory context. Ambiguous technical thresholds and exceptions could make the required mental state especially difficult to prove.

52. **§§ 2(1)(B), 5 — Designation timing creates penalty uncertainty.** The bill does not specify whether designation operates only prospectively or how existing operators receive notice and cease covered conduct. Attempting to punish predesignation conduct under the capability prong would raise substantial fair-notice concerns.

53. **§§ 5(a), 8 — Civil penalty timing conflicts with the effective date.** Section 5(a) refers to violations on or after enactment, but section 8 delays the Act’s effectiveness for 180 days. The inconsistent dates invite litigation over whether any duty or penalty applies during that interval.

### Section 6 — International agreement

54. **§ 6 — The deadline and required result are ambiguous.** “Shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months” does not clearly require negotiations to begin, conclude, or produce an agreement by that date. No reporting requirement or fallback follows failure to secure agreement.

55. **§ 6 — “Equivalent” prohibitions could replicate the domestic loopholes.** An agreement could preserve broad grandfathering and safety exceptions while still being equivalent to section 3. The provision also omits required participation, verification, enforcement, and treatment of nonparticipating jurisdictions.

56. **§ 6 — Negotiation does not itself establish enforceable international restrictions.** The bill supplies no implementation mechanism, interim controls on foreign work, or consequences for relocation to nonparticipating countries. It also does not specify the agreement’s intended legal form or any necessary subsequent congressional action.

### Sections 7–8 — Duration and commencement

57. **§ 7(a) — The safety finding has no defined substantive standard.** “Can be developed safely” leaves acceptable risk, scope of evidence, deployment safety, and required conditions unspecified. A finding that one restricted development method is safe could be invoked to end the prohibition generally.

58. **§ 7(a) — The National Academies report is not commissioned or specified.** No provision directs or funds a report, sets its scope, establishes independence requirements, or requires a favorable conclusion. Congress need only act “on” a report, not necessarily follow its findings.

59. **§ 7(a) — Ending the prohibition need not establish a replacement regime.** The prohibition could terminate without enforceable requirements for the safeguards underlying the safety finding. There is no conditional licensing framework, continuing monitoring requirement for developers, or reinstatement trigger.

60. **§ 7(a) — The joint-resolution mechanism should expressly require enactment.** Joint resolutions ordinarily require bicameral passage and presentment, but “finds by joint resolution” should make that requirement explicit. Any interpretation allowing Congress to change binding law without presentment would create a constitutional problem.

61. **§§ 7(a)–(b) — The sunset defeats the apparent safety prerequisite.** Section 7(a) suggests the prohibition lasts until Congress makes a safety finding, but section 7(b) ends the entire Act after ten years regardless. Companies could simply wait for expiration, and the registry would expire too.

62. **§ 7(b) — Post-sunset enforcement and records handling are not addressed.** The bill does not expressly preserve pending proceedings, accrued liabilities, or necessary record retention and agency authority. The general federal saving statute may preserve some liabilities, but the bill should not leave the full transition to default rules.

63. **§ 8 — The 180-day delay permits substantial additional development.** No prohibition or registry duty clearly applies during that period, and no interim authority prevents companies from completing or deploying systems before commencement. Systems whose training began after enactment would not qualify for grandfathering, but enforcement would still start only after the delay.

64. **§§ 4, 8 — There is no implementation timetable aligned with commencement.** Commerce receives no specific deadlines to establish registration procedures, reporting formats, compute-accounting rules, or designation procedures. The substantive ban could commence before the compliance and enforcement machinery is operational.

### Cross-cutting

65. **Act-wide — Federal actors and sovereign immunity are not expressly addressed.** “Any person” does not unambiguously resolve coverage of federal agencies or government-operated programs, and the bill contains no express waiver permitting penalties against the federal government. If government development is intended to be prohibited, that requires clear treatment.

66. **Act-wide — Severability is not addressed.** If a court invalidates a definition, designation mechanism, or application of the prohibition, the statute provides no express direction to preserve the remaining provisions. A severability clause would reduce—but not eliminate—the risk that one successful challenge disables unrelated parts of the Act.
